First Warn Forecast

Wednesday, August 12, 2026

Dangerous Heat Continues
Severe Storms Possible This Afternoon
Better Relief May Arrive Early Next Week

Dangerous heat and humidity will remain firmly in place across the region today and Thursday. The Heat Advisory and Extreme Heat Warning have now been extended through 8 p.m. Thursday, and another extension into the weekend remains possible.

Temperatures today should be slightly lower than what we experienced Tuesday, with highs generally in the lower to middle 90s. Even so, dew points in the lower 70s will keep it very humid, and afternoon heat index values will still climb into the 100 to 105 degree range.

Across northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois, cloud cover and nearby thunderstorms may hold temperatures in the upper 80s in some locations. However, that will not necessarily make it feel much better. Less mixing in the atmosphere could keep dew points even higher, maintaining that very muggy feel.

The dangerous heat continues Thursday. Forecast guidance shows a very high probability of temperatures reaching at least 95 degrees, with dew points remaining above 70. That combination will once again produce dangerous afternoon heat index values.

Continue to take the heat seriously. Limit prolonged outdoor activity during the hottest part of the day, drink plenty of water, check on those who may be more vulnerable to the heat, and make sure pets have shade and fresh water.

Severe Storm Threat This Afternoon

Our attention also turns to the potential for strong to severe thunderstorms later today.

A complex of thunderstorms currently moving across portions of South Dakota and Nebraska will track east-southeast along the edge of the large ridge of high pressure. While the main thunderstorm complex is expected to pass north of our area through southeastern Iowa and northern Illinois, it could send an outflow boundary southward into eastern Missouri and western Illinois this afternoon.

That boundary may be enough to trigger isolated thunderstorms in our area.

The atmosphere will certainly have plenty of fuel available, with substantial instability and abundant low-level moisture. The main limiting factor is a lack of stronger large-scale forcing, so widespread thunderstorm development is not expected.

Instead, storms should remain fairly isolated, developing where the outflow boundary can provide enough lift to overcome the cap in the atmosphere.

The greatest chance for thunderstorm development appears to be across southwestern Illinois during the middle and late afternoon. An isolated storm could develop farther north into northeastern Missouri or west-central Illinois somewhat earlier.

Any storm that develops could become strong quickly.

The primary severe weather threat will be damaging wind gusts. Dry air higher in the atmosphere could enhance thunderstorm downdrafts, allowing strong winds to reach the surface.

A brief tornado cannot be completely ruled out, particularly during the middle afternoon when low-level wind shear may briefly become more favorable. The tornado threat appears limited, but it is something we will be watching.

The Storm Prediction Center has placed much of Illinois and far eastern Missouri in a Slight Risk for severe thunderstorms, while the remainder of the Missouri portion of the region remains in a Marginal Risk.

This is not expected to be a widespread severe weather outbreak. Most locations may not see a thunderstorm at all. However, any storm that does develop this afternoon could produce damaging winds, frequent lightning, heavy rainfall and possibly a brief tornado.

Another Rain Chance Thursday Night Into Friday

Another round of showers and thunderstorms may develop Thursday night into Friday as moisture pools along a stationary front across the Midwest.

The heaviest rainfall is currently expected to remain north of our region, primarily across Iowa, northern Illinois and into northern Indiana.

Northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois will have the better opportunity for rain locally. Current guidance suggests roughly a 25 to 50 percent chance of receiving at least one-quarter inch of rainfall in those areas.

Rain chances drop considerably farther south. The St. Louis metropolitan area currently has only about a 10 to 20 percent chance of receiving more than one-tenth of an inch.

As always with summertime thunderstorms, localized rainfall amounts could be higher depending on exactly where storms develop and track.

Heat Builds Back Into the Weekend

Unfortunately, any rain we receive does not appear likely to bring lasting relief from the heat.

The large ridge of high pressure is expected to strengthen northward again late this week, keeping the hot and humid air mass in place through the weekend.

Forecast guidance currently shows a 75 to 90 percent chance of high temperatures reaching at least 95 degrees Friday through Sunday. Dew points are also likely to remain above 70, meaning heat index values could once again become dangerously high.

That is why an additional extension of the current heat headlines into Friday or the weekend remains possible.

There is, however, some encouraging news showing up in the longer-range forecast.

Guidance continues to indicate that a stronger cold front may finally move through the region late Sunday into Monday. Falling upper-level heights and a developing northerly flow would help push the persistent heat and humidity southward.

There are still details to work out, but confidence continues to increase that more meaningful relief could arrive early next week.

For today, we are dealing with two weather concerns. The dangerous heat continues, and isolated strong to severe thunderstorms could develop this afternoon, especially across Illinois and far eastern Missouri.

Keep an eye on the sky, have a way to receive weather warnings, and continue taking precautions from the heat.

First. Accurate. Trusted.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
